messages.content: I have a Google Pixel phone and I can't hear it ring from the other room. How do I make the ringer louder?

You can turn the ringer up with the buttons on the side of your phone.

1. Press one of the **volume buttons** on the side of your phone.
2. A small volume bar appears on the screen. Tap the **Menu** icon at the right.
3. Find **Ring Volume** and slide it up to make the ring louder.

If you don't see a **Menu** icon, your phone has older software. Tap the **Down arrow** at the right instead, then slide **Ring**.

If your phone was set to vibrate or mute, tap the **Ring** icon above the slider, then turn off **Vibrate** or turn on **Ring** to bring the sound back.

messages.content: My iPhone has no home button, you just look at it to unlock it. How do I take a screenshot of my boarding pass?

On your iPhone you take a screenshot with two buttons on the sides.

1. Open the screen you want to capture, such as your boarding pass.

Those add-ons (called extensions) could be the cause. You can check them one at a time.

1. Turn off one extension in your browser.
2. Open Gmail again and see if it loads.
3. If it still does not load, turn off the next extension and open Gmail again. Repeat until Gmail loads.

You can also try a private browsing window, if your browser has one (it may be called incognito), and open Gmail there.

If you turn off an extension and Gmail loads, that extension was the cause.

messages.content: My printer is plugged into my Windows computer with a USB cable but nothing comes out when I press print. What should I check?

Let's start with two simple things.

3. Plug the printer back in and turn it on.
4. Check the USB cable. Make sure it is firmly connected at both ends, on the printer and on the computer.

messages.content: My grandson just called crying. He said he got arrested and needs me to buy $2,000 in gift cards and read him the numbers. He said not to tell his mom. What should I do?

I'm sorry, that must have been frightening. Please **don't buy the gift cards yet**. This has several signs of a common scam where someone pretends to be a grandchild in trouble:

- They need money **right away**
- They want **gift cards**, a way of paying that scammers like because it is hard to get your money back
- They ask you to **keep it a secret**

Here's what to do:

1. Don't buy anything right away. Resist the urge to act immediately, no matter how dramatic the story may be.
2. Call your grandson using the phone number **you already have for him**, not a number the caller gave you.
3. Call his mom or another family member too, even though the caller said not to.

If it really was him, your family can help sort it out. If it was a scammer, you can report it at **www.ftc.gov/complaint**.

If you already bought cards or read any numbers to them, tell me right away and I'll help you with the next steps.

messages.content: I got a Facebook message from someone who says she is my granddaughter Emily. I want to help her but I'm not sure. What should I do?

I'm glad you stopped to ask. **Please don't wire any money yet.** Scammers often pretend to be a grandchild in trouble, and they push for payment right away.

1. Take a breath. You don't have to act right now, even if the story sounds dramatic.
2. Call Emily on a phone number **you know is really hers**. Don't use any number from the message.
3. Check the story with another trusted family member too.
4. Don't wire money, pay with a gift card, or send cash for an emergency request.

You can report the message at **www.ftc.gov/complaint**.

messages.content: My iPhone has no signal in my basement apartment but I have Wi-Fi. Can I make calls using the Wi-Fi?

iPhone has a feature called **Wi-Fi Calling** that lets you make calls over Wi-Fi when there is little or no cellular coverage. Turning it on takes about a minute.

1. Open the **Settings** app.
2. Tap **Cellular**.
3. Tap **Wi-Fi Calling**.
4. Turn on **Wi-Fi Calling on This iPhone**.
5. Tap **Enable** when asked.

Your iPhone may ask you to enter or confirm your address. This address is used for emergency services, so please enter it carefully.

Wi-Fi Calling only works if your phone company offers it. To see that it's working, open Control Center. If Wi-Fi Calling is available, you'll see **Wi-Fi** in the status bar there. Then you make calls the same way you always do.

If you don't see **Wi-Fi Calling** in that menu, your phone company may not offer it. Tell me what you see, and you can also ask your phone company.

messages.content: How do I take a screenshot on my Android phone?

1. Get the screen showing what you want to capture.

messages.content: How do I take a screenshot on my Windows 11 laptop?

The quickest way uses three keys at once. It takes a few seconds.

1. Press and hold the **Windows logo key** and the **Shift** key, then press **S**.
2. The screen dims and shows a few capture choices.
3. Choose the shape you want: a rectangle, a window, or the full screen.
4. If you chose rectangle, click and drag over the part of the screen you want.

Your screenshot is saved automatically in your **Screenshots** folder.

**Another option:** press the **Print Screen** key (often labeled **PrtSc**). This copies the whole screen, but it isn't saved as a file until you paste it somewhere, like an email.

messages.content: How do I update the software on my Android phone?

Here's how to check for an update. Before you start, connect to Wi-Fi and make sure your battery is at least 75% charged, because updates can take a while.

1. Open the **Settings** app.
2. Tap **System**.
3. Tap **Software updates**. The update status appears there. Names can be a little different on some phones.

messages.content: I just bought a new printer. How do I add it to my Windows 11 computer?

Here's how to add your new printer. It can take a few minutes.

**First:** turn the printer on. If it uses a cable, plug it into the computer. Some printers, especially ones with a cable, install by themselves once they are plugged in and on. If it's wireless, make sure it's on the same Wi-Fi network as your computer.

7. When your printer appears, click **Add device** next to it.

If your printer doesn't show up, look for **The printer that I want isn't listed**, choose **Add a new device manually**, and follow the instructions.

messages.content: I forgot my Gmail password and can't sign in. How do I get back into my account?

You can get back in through Google's account recovery. It usually takes a few minutes.

1. Go to **accounts.google.com/signin/recovery** (Google's account recovery page).
2. Answer the questions it asks to show the account is yours. Answer as accurately as you can, and if you're not sure, make your best guess. A wrong guess doesn't end the process, and you can try again.
3. When asked, create a **new password** that you haven't used for this account before.

**Stay safe while you do this:**
- Google staff can't help you sign in over the phone, so ignore anyone who calls or messages offering to recover your account.
- Never share your password or any verification code with anyone.

If you recently changed your recovery info, it can take up to 7 days to take effect, so try again after a few days.

messages.content: My granddaughter called crying and said she's in jail and needs bail money wired right now. It really sounded like her. Is this real?

Please **don't send any money yet**. Scammers can now copy a person's voice from a short recording, like a video posted online, so a call can sound exactly like someone you love.

**Warning sign:** Scammers ask you to pay in ways that make it hard to get your money back: wire money, cryptocurrency, or gift cards.

If it turns out to be a scam, you can report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**. If you already sent money, tell me right away and we'll work out the next steps.

Let's check it together. For now, **please don't click any link or give any information** in that text. **What does the text ask you to do?**
It has a link and says I need to pay $1.99 for redelivery.

Thanks. A small fee plus a link is a very common sign of a scam, even when you really are expecting a package. Please **don't click the link**. It usually leads to a fake website that looks real and asks for your personal or card information.

Instead:

1. **Don't click** the link or reply.
2. Check on your package using the website or app of the **store where you bought it**. Go there directly, not through the text.
3. **Report the text.** Use your phone's **junk** or **spam** reporting option if you see one, or forward the text to **7726**. You can also report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.
4. Then delete it.

If you already clicked and typed in your card number, call your bank right away using the number on the back of your card.

messages.content: I'm expecting about four packages this week from different places, so a text from USPS about a package problem could be real. It wants me to tap a link to confirm my delivery preferences. I don't remember which store each package came from.

Please **don't tap the link** or give any information, even with several packages on the way. The link usually goes to a look-alike of a real website that asks for personal or payment details, and anything you enter goes to the scammer.

1. **Don't click** the link or reply.
2. **Check each order where you bought it.** Open the website or account of each store you ordered from, and look up the shipping and tracking information there, not through the text.
3. **Report the text.** Use your messaging app's junk or spam option, or forward it to **7726**.
4. You can also report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

I'm sorry, these texts look very real and fool many people. Contact your credit card company right away.

1. **Report it to the credit card issuer immediately.** Call the number on the back of your card, or log in to your account online or in the app.
2. Tell them what happened and **ask for a refund**.

4. **Report it to the FTC** at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

messages.content: I got an email from my pastor asking me to buy five $100 gift cards for church members and send him the numbers on the back. He said he's in a meeting and can't talk. Should I do it?

Please **don't buy the gift cards**. This is a common scam. Real businesses, government agencies, and people you know don't ask to be paid with gift card numbers, and once you share the numbers, the money is very hard to get back.

Here's what to do:

1. **Don't reply** to the email.
2. **Call your pastor** using a phone number you already have, or call the church office, and ask if he really sent it.
3. If it's fake, you can report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

**If you already bought cards and shared the numbers:**
- Call the **gift card company** right away and ask for your money back. Sometimes they can freeze what's left on the card.
- Keep the cards and the store receipt.
- Report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.
Oh no. I already bought two $100 cards this morning and emailed him the numbers before I saw this.

I'm sorry this happened. This scam fools a lot of careful people. Acting quickly gives you the best chance of getting money back.

1. **Contact the gift card company right away.** Tell them the cards were used in a scam and ask for your money back. Sometimes they can freeze money that hasn't been spent yet. The FTC's gift card scam page lists contact information for major gift card companies.
2. **Keep the cards and the store receipt**, and take a photo of both. You'll need them when you report it.
3. **Report the scam** at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.
4. **Don't reply** to the email, and don't buy more cards, even if you're asked again.
5. **Tell your church office**, so they can warn other members, and let your pastor know his email may have been hacked.

Do you have the cards and the receipt with you? If so, we can look at step 1 together.

messages.content: How do I set up Family Sharing on my iPhone so my daughter can be part of it?

**Create the group:**

3. Follow the instructions on the screen to set up your family group and invite members.

**To invite your daughter later, or if you skipped that:**
4. Go to **Settings**, then **Family**.
5. Tap the **Add Member** button.
6. Tap **Invite Others** and follow the steps to send her an invitation.

Once she accepts, she'll be part of your family group. If she doesn't see the invitation, go to **Settings**, then **Family**, tap her name, and choose **Resend Invitation**.

messages.content: My iPhone battery seems to die quickly. How do I check the battery health?

You can check it in Settings. It takes a minute.

1. Open the **Settings** app.
2. Tap **Battery**.
3. Tap **Battery Health**. On some versions the name is slightly different.
4. Look at **Maximum Capacity**. This compares your battery now to when it was new. A lower number means it won't last as long between charges.

If you see a message that your battery's health is **significantly degraded**, it isn't a safety problem, but a new battery would help it last longer. Apple offers battery service, and it may be covered if your phone is still under warranty.

messages.content: How do I delete an app I don't use anymore from my iPhone?

Here's how. It takes a few seconds.

1. Find the app on your Home Screen.
2. **Press and hold** the app's icon until a menu appears.
3. Tap **Remove App**.
4. Tap **Delete App**.
5. Tap **Delete** to confirm.

If the icons start to jiggle instead of showing a menu:
1. Tap the **minus** sign in the app's upper-left corner.
2. Tap **Delete App**.
3. Tap **Delete**.
4. Tap **Done** at the top of the screen.

Deleting an app also removes its data from your phone.

Deleting an app does **not** cancel any paid subscriptions inside it. If you pay for the app every month, cancel the subscription first.

messages.content: How do I set an alarm on my iPhone for 6:30 in the morning?

Here's how. It takes about a minute.

1. Open the **Clock** app, then tap the **Alarms** tab.
2. Tap the **Add** button.
3. Set the time to **6:30 AM**.

If the alarm is too quiet, go to **Settings**, then **Sounds & Haptics**, and drag the **Ringtone and Alerts** slider to the right. If it only vibrates, check that the alarm's **Sound** isn't set to **None**.

messages.content: I just got new hearing aids that work with iPhone. How do I connect them?

Here's how to pair them. It takes a few minutes.

1. Make sure your iPhone has the latest software update.
2. Put your hearing aids in **pairing mode**. Depending on the model, you might open and close the battery doors, turn them off and on, or take them out of the charger. Your hearing aid instructions will say which.
3. On your iPhone, open **Settings**.
4. Tap **Accessibility**.
5. Tap **Hearing Devices**.
6. Tap **Pair MFi Hearing Device** and follow the steps on the screen.
7. Select your hearing aids, then tap **Pair**.

If you don't see **Pair MFi Hearing Device**, tap your hearing aids' name when it appears under **Hearing Devices**, then tap **Pair**.

If they don't appear, check that they're in pairing mode, restart your iPhone, and look in your hearing aids' user guide or the maker's app.

messages.content: Is there a way to zoom in on my Android phone's screen to read small things?

Android has a **Magnification** feature. Setting it up takes a couple of minutes.

**Turn it on:**
1. Open **Settings**.
2. Tap **Accessibility**.
3. Tap **Magnification**.
4. Turn on the **Magnification shortcut**. You can choose how to start it: the **Accessibility button** on the screen, **pressing and holding both volume keys**, or **triple-tapping** the screen.

**Use it:**
1. Start magnification with your shortcut.
2. Tap anywhere on the screen, except the keyboard or the navigation bar.
3. **Pinch** with two fingers to zoom in or out.
4. **Drag with two fingers** to move around.
5. Use the shortcut again to stop.

It can zoom up to 8 times.

messages.content: How do I set up Medical ID on my iPhone so paramedics can see my allergies?

Medical ID lets first responders see your important health information from the Lock Screen, without your passcode.

1. Open the **Health** app.
2. Tap **Summary**.
3. Tap your **profile picture** in the upper corner.
4. Tap **Medical ID**.
5. Turn on **Show When Locked** so it can be seen from the Lock Screen.

Keep in mind that anyone holding your phone can see this information, so only add what you're comfortable sharing.

messages.content: I met a man online three months ago. He says he loves me, he works on an oil rig overseas, and now he needs $2,000 for a plane ticket to come see me. Should I send it?

I'm glad you asked before sending anything. Please **don't send the money**. What you're describing matches a very common scam called a **romance scam**.

**Warning signs:**
- The person can't meet in person, often saying they work far away, like on an **oil rig** or in the military.
- Strong feelings grow quickly through lots of messages.
- Now there's a **need for money**, like travel costs or an emergency.

**What to do:**
1. **Don't send money or gift cards** to someone you haven't met in person.
2. **Talk to a friend or family member** you trust. People close to you can often spot things that are hard to see from the inside.
3. You can **search his photo** online to see if it appears under other names. I can show you how.
4. If it's a scam, stop contact and report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov** and to the website or app where you met.

If you've already sent money, contact your bank or the payment company right away and ask for a refund.

messages.content: A caller said he's from Social Security and my number has been suspended because of a crime. He wants me to buy gift cards to fix it. What should I do?

Please **hang up and don't pay anything**. This is a scam. The real Social Security Administration **won't threaten you, won't suspend your Social Security number, and won't ask you to pay with gift cards**.

**What to do:**
1. **Hang up.** Don't share any personal or bank information.
2. Don't trust caller ID. Scammers can make it show a government name or number.
3. If you're worried, **call Social Security yourself** using the phone number on its official website, not a number the caller gave you.
4. **Report the call** to the Social Security Administration's Office of the Inspector General and to the FTC at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

If you already shared your Social Security number or bank details, go to **IdentityTheft.gov** for next steps, and tell me so I can help.

messages.content: I'm making a new password for my insurance company's website and it keeps rejecting my long phrase of words because it has a length limit. I also don't trust password manager programs and don't want one. How can I still make a strong password?

You can still make a strong one without a password manager. When a site rejects long passwords, **mix different kinds of characters** instead.

1. Use **uppercase and lowercase letters**, **numbers**, and **symbols** together.
2. Make it as long as the site allows. Aim for at least 12 characters if you can.
3. Don't use a common phrase, song lyric, or movie quote.

Your **email** password matters most, because password reset links often go to your email inbox.

1. At the store, **create a new strong password**. Make it long, at least 12 characters. Several random words work well.
2. Change the password on your **email** and your **bank** account too, since they share the old one.
3. If you see that someone is using your personal information, get help at **IdentityTheft.gov**.

Email is the most important one to protect, because password reset links often go there.

messages.content: What is Stolen Device Protection on iPhone and how do I turn it on?

Stolen Device Protection adds extra security if someone steals your iPhone **and** knows your passcode. When your phone is away from familiar places like home or work, it requires **Face ID or Touch ID** for things like using saved passwords, and it adds a **one-hour wait** before important changes, like changing your Apple Account password.

**To turn it on:**
1. Open **Settings**.
2. Tap **Face ID & Passcode** (or **Touch ID & Passcode**).
3. Enter your passcode.
4. Tap **Stolen Device Protection** and turn it on.

It may already be on, so check first.

It needs a few things to work: an iPhone updated to **iOS 17.3 or later**, a passcode, Face ID or Touch ID, two-factor authentication on your Apple Account, **Find My** turned on, and **Significant Locations** turned on in Location Services.

messages.content: Why does my iPhone stop charging at 80% overnight? Is something wrong with it?

Most likely nothing is wrong. This is usually a feature called **Optimized Battery Charging**. It holds the battery at 80% during long charges, like overnight, to slow down battery wear. Your iPhone then finishes charging around the time you usually unplug it.

A couple of other things can also stop charging at 80%:
- **Heat:** if your iPhone gets too warm, it may pause charging above 80%. Moving it to a cooler spot helps.
- **Charge limit:** on iPhone 15 and newer, a charge limit setting may be turned on. You can change it if you want a full charge.

If you need a full charge right away, tell me and I'll walk you through it.

messages.content: My iPhone only vibrates when someone calls. It doesn't ring. How do I fix that?

Your iPhone is probably in **Silent mode**. Here's how to check.

**If your iPhone has a small switch on the side** (above the volume buttons):
1. Look at the switch. If you see **orange**, Silent mode is on.
2. Flip the switch so the orange no longer shows.

**If your iPhone has an Action button instead** (iPhone 15 Pro and newer):
1. **Press and hold** the **Action button** until you see Silent mode turn off at the top of the screen. By default, this button turns Silent mode on and off. If it's been set to do something else, tell me and we'll check another way.

Once Silent mode is off, your phone will ring again. If it's still too quiet, press the **volume up** button while you're on the Home Screen.

messages.content: My iPhone screen keeps turning sideways when I'm reading in bed. How do I make it stay upright?

messages.content: My iPhone is frozen and won't respond when I touch it. What do I do?

You can **force restart** it. The steps depend on your model.

**iPhone with Face ID (no Home button):**
1. Press and quickly release the **volume up** button.
2. Press and quickly release the **volume down** button.
3. Press and **hold** the **side button** until you see the **Apple logo**. This can take more than 10 seconds, so keep holding.

**iPhone 7:** press and hold the **side button** and **volume down** together until you see the Apple logo.

**iPhone 6s or older (with a Home button):** press and hold the **Home button** and the **side or top button** together for about 10 seconds, until you see the Apple logo.

If it still won't turn on, charge it for an hour and try again.

messages.content: My iPhone won't charge when I plug it in. What should I try?

Let's go through a few checks. This can take up to an hour, mostly waiting.

1. **Restart your iPhone.**
2. **Check the cable and adapter** for damage, like breakage or bent prongs. Don't use a damaged one.
3. **Plug into a wall outlet** and make sure the cable, adapter, and outlet are firmly connected, or try a different outlet.
4. **Look in the charging port** on the bottom of the phone. If there's lint or dirt, carefully clear it out, then plug in firmly again.
5. **Leave it charging for half an hour.**
6. If it still won't turn on or only shows a battery picture, **force restart** it. On an iPhone 8 or later:
   - Press and quickly release **volume up**.
   - Press and quickly release **volume down**.
   - Press and hold the **side button** until you see the **Apple logo**.
   On an older iPhone, tell me the model and I'll give you those steps.
7. **Charge it for another half hour.**

If none of this works, it may need service from Apple.

**If it stops at 80%:** that's usually a battery-saving feature, not a problem.

messages.content: How can I make my Android phone save a copy of everything automatically?

messages.content: A man I met online says he is an investment manager and wants me to buy cryptocurrency and send it to his site. He says I will make a lot of money. Is this real?

Please do not buy or send any cryptocurrency. This is very likely a scam.

Scammers promise easy profits and steer people to send crypto to a fake investment account. The site can look real, but you may never be able to take your money out.

1. Do not click any more links from him or pay him.
2. Search his name and the crypto name with words like **review**, **scam**, or **complaint**.
3. Report him at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

Nobody can truly guarantee profits.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: What To Know About Cryptocurrency and Scams

messages.content: I got a text yesterday saying it was from the power company. It said my account has a legal problem and I have to buy cryptocurrency and send it today or they will shut off my power. I am a widow and I live alone and I am scared. I have not done anything yet. What should I do?

Do not pay, and do not click the link in that text. Only scammers demand payment in cryptocurrency.

Scammers pretend to be utilities or government offices, claim there is a problem, and tell you to buy crypto to fix it. You have done nothing wrong.

1. Do not click any links in the text, even if it looks like it is from a company you know.
2. Do not send any money to the person who contacted you.
3. Report the text at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: What To Know About Cryptocurrency and Scams

messages.content: A woman on a dating app has been teaching me to invest in crypto. Her website shows my money has doubled. She says I must add more by tonight or I lose my profits, but when I tried to take some out it would not let me. What do I do?

Do not add any more money. This looks like an investment scam.

The site can look real but be fake, and scammers often make it hard to withdraw. A love interest who gives investment advice is a warning sign, and so is pressure to pay someone who contacted you first.

1. Stop sending money and stop clicking her links.
2. Report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.
3. You can also report it at **sec.gov/tcr** and **CFTC.gov/complaint**.
4. If you sent crypto already, contact the exchange you used.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: What To Know About Cryptocurrency and Scams

messages.content: My mother says someone who emailed her out of the blue is going to help her invest in a new coin. She wants to buy cryptocurrency and send it to him. How can I help her?

1. Ask her not to click links in that email or pay him.
2. Together, search his name and the coin name with words like **review**, **scam**, or **complaint**.

4. If she already sent crypto, contact the exchange she used.

messages.content: How can I tell if a crypto investment offer is a scam, and where do I report one?

Never pay anyone who contacts you out of the blue and asks for crypto. Only scammers demand payment in cryptocurrency.

Warning signs:
1. Guaranteed profits or big, quick returns.
2. Unexpected contact from a company, agency, or "investment manager".
3. A love interest who gives investment advice or asks for money.
4. Vague explanations of how the investment works.

Do not click links in unexpected texts, emails, or social media messages. Before investing, search the name and the crypto name with words like **review**, **scam**, or **complaint**.

To report, go to **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: What To Know About Cryptocurrency and Scams

messages.content: I already sent a lot of cryptocurrency to a person I met on social media for an investment. Now they want more money to let me withdraw. Can I get my money back?

Do not send anything more. I am sorry this happened. It is not your fault.

Crypto payments are usually not reversible. You can generally only get the money back if the person who received it sends it back, so please act quickly on these steps.

1. Contact the crypto exchange you used to send the money.
2. Report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.
3. Also report it at **CFTC.gov/complaint**, **sec.gov/tcr**, and **ic3.gov/Home/FileComplaint**.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: What To Know About Cryptocurrency and Scams

messages.content: How do I update the software on my MacBook?

Here is how to update your Mac.

1. Click the **Apple** menu at the top left of the screen and choose **System Settings**.
2. Click **General** in the sidebar.
3. Click **Software Update** on the right. Your Mac checks for updates by itself.
4. If an update is shown, click the button to update, upgrade, or restart now.
5. If asked, type your administrator password. This is the password you use to log in to your Mac.
6. Let it finish. Do not let the Mac go to sleep or close its lid. It may restart a few times and show a progress bar or a blank screen.

It is a good idea to back up your Mac before you install new software.

messages.content: How do I delete a game I downloaded from the internet on my Mac? I do not play it anymore.

Here is how to remove it.

1. If the game is open, quit it first.
2. Open a **Finder** window and click **Applications** in the sidebar.
3. Find the game. If it came with an app called **Uninstall** or **Uninstaller**, open that and follow it. That also removes the extra files it left behind.
4. If there is no uninstaller, drag the game to the **Trash**.
5. If asked, type your administrator name and password. This is usually what you use to log in.
6. In the menu bar, choose **Finder**, then **Empty Trash**. This deletes it for good and frees up space.

messages.content: The Mail app on my iPhone will not send or get any email. What should I do?

Try these first, in order, and stop when your email works.

1. Make sure your iPhone is connected to the internet.
2. Check your email provider's status page, or contact them, to see if there is an outage.
3. In a web browser, sign in to your provider's website to confirm your email address and password.
4. Ask your provider if two-step verification is turned on. You may need a special password from them to use email on your iPhone.
5. Open **Settings**, then tap **Apps**.
6. Tap **Mail**, then tap **Mail Accounts**.
7. Tap **Fetch New Data**, then choose **Automatically**, **Manually**, or a schedule.

Last resort, only if nothing above works: removing the account can delete emails already saved on your phone. So first, on a computer, sign in to your provider's website and make sure all your email is there or saved somewhere other than the phone. Then:

1. Open **Settings**, tap **Apps**, then tap **Mail**.
2. Tap **Mail Accounts**, tap your account, then tap **Delete Account**.
3. Add the account again.

If that does not help, contact your email provider.

messages.content: My Google Pixel phone won't charge. I plug it in and nothing seems to happen.

Let's check the usual causes.

1. Take the phone case off so it does not block the plug.
2. Make sure the cable is pushed in firmly at both ends, the adapter and the phone.
3. Look in the phone's charging port for dust or lint.
4. Try a different cable or adapter, and a different wall outlet.
5. Leave it plugged in for one minute. A battery icon on the screen means the phone is off and charging.
6. Press and hold the **Power** button for 5 to 7 seconds.

A very low battery can take several minutes before the screen turns on.

1. Plug it into a working wall outlet with a firmly connected cable and adapter.
2. Press and hold the **Power** button for 5 to 7 seconds.
3. Keep it plugged in. You may see no charging icon, no vibration, and no screen response for up to 25 minutes.

If there is still no response after 25 minutes, the phone needs to be repaired.

messages.content: My Android phone says it has no internet. Web pages won't load. What should I do?

Try these in order.

1. Restart your phone.
2. Open **Settings** and tap **Network & internet** (on some phones it is called **Connections**).
3. Turn Wi-Fi off and mobile data on, and see if things load. If not, turn mobile data off and Wi-Fi on, and check again.
4. Turn **Airplane mode** on, wait 10 seconds, then turn it off.
5. If you use home Wi-Fi, unplug the router, wait 30 seconds, plug it back in, and wait about 30 seconds for the lights to come back.

If problems continue, contact your mobile service provider or your internet provider.

messages.content: Hi, I'm at home and my Android phone shows the Wi-Fi at the top but nothing will open, not the weather, not my email. My daughter's tablet in the next room is fine though, or at least it was an hour ago. I've had the same Wi-Fi for years. I restarted the phone once already. What else can I try?

Here is what to try next for Wi-Fi.

1. Open **Settings** and tap **Network & Internet** (or **Connections**), then tap **Wi-Fi**.
2. Make sure **Wi-Fi** is turned on.
3. Look at the Wi-Fi symbol at the top of the screen. If it is missing or has no bars filled, you may be out of range. Move closer to the router and try again.
4. Restart the router. Unplug it and make sure the lights go out. Wait 30 seconds, plug it back in, and wait about 30 seconds for all the lights to come back.

If it still does not work, contact your internet provider.

4. Look for 2G, 3G, 4G, or H next to the signal bars at the top of the screen.
5. If you see none, you may be out of coverage. Move somewhere else, or go outside, and check again.

If this happens often, contact your mobile service provider.

messages.content: None of my texts are going through in Google Messages on my Android phone. What should I check?

Check these in order.

1. Update **Google Messages** to the newest version.
2. If your phone has a SIM card, make sure it is inserted properly.
3. Set **Google Messages** as your default texting app.
4. Check that your plan or credit balance covers sending and receiving texts.
5. Check that you have signal.
6. If airplane mode is on, turn it off.

Also check that your carrier supports SMS, MMS, or RCS.

messages.content: I sold my old camera online and the buyer mailed me a check for more than the price. He wants me to send him back the extra. Is that okay?

Please do not send him anything. This is a common trick: the extra money is the bait, and the check is likely fake.

1. Do not accept a check for more than the selling price.
2. Do not send back the difference, by any method.
3. Fake checks can look real, even to bank workers, and it can take weeks for a bank to find the fraud.
4. Report it to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

If the check was already deposited, remember that seeing the money in your account does not mean the check is good. If it is fake, you may have to repay the bank.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: Fake check scams

messages.content: I got an email saying I was picked to be a mystery shopper for a money transfer store. They mailed me a big check and told me to deposit it, keep a little for myself, and wire the rest to a man they named. I went to the bank and the teller said the money is already showing in my account. I really need the extra money right now. Should I wire it?

No, please do not wire any of it. Wiring money from a check to someone who asks is a classic fake check scam.

1. Never use money from a check to wire money to anyone who asks.
2. Do not rely on money from a check unless you know and trust the person who sent it.
3. Report it to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

Banks must make deposited funds available quickly, so seeing the money in your account does not mean the check is good. If it turns out to be fake, you may have to repay the bank.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: Fake check scams

messages.content: The check I deposited cleared and the bank website shows the full amount as available, so it must be real. The sender keeps texting that I need to send back the extra today, and that I shouldn't bother anyone at the bank about it. Can I just send it?

No, please do not send it. Money showing as available does not make the check good.

1. Banks must make deposited funds available quickly by law, even when the check is fake.
2. It can take weeks for a bank to find the fraud, and then you may have to repay the bank.
3. Do not send any of the money back, no matter how urgent the texts sound.
4. Report it to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

Even if you see the funds in your account, that does not mean the check is good.

messages.content: My grandfather got a check in the mail from a company that wants to put an ad wrap on his car. They told him to deposit it and then pay the installers out of it. He is excited. What should I tell him?

Tell him not to pay anyone from that check. This is a known fake check scam called car wrap decals.

1. Ask him not to deposit and spend money, or send any to the installers.
2. Explain that fake checks often look real, even to bank workers.
3. Remind him that a bank can find the fraud weeks later, and then he may have to repay it.
4. Help him report it to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

If he already sent money, tell me how and I can help with the next step.

messages.content: How can I spot a fake check scam before I fall for one, and where do I report it?

Here are the warning signs and the rules to follow.

1. Be wary if you are asked to wire money, buy gift cards, or buy cryptocurrency. Gift cards are for gifts, not payments.
2. Be wary if a check is for more than the selling price, or you are asked to pay fees to get a prize.
3. Never use money from a check to buy gift cards or money orders, buy cryptocurrency, or wire money.
4. Do not rely on money from a check unless you know and trust the person.

To report one, go to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov, the U.S. Postal Inspection Service at uspis.gov/report, or your state Attorney General.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: Fake check scams

messages.content: A man mailed me a check and said to deposit it and buy gift cards with the money for his company. I already bought the cards and sent him the numbers on the back. Now my bank says the check was fake. What do I do?

I am sorry, this happens to many people. Act quickly on the gift cards.

1. Contact the company that issued each gift card right away.
2. Tell them the card was used in a scam and ask for a refund.
3. Tell the store where you bought the cards.
4. Report it to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

Because the check was fake, you may have to repay the bank.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: Fake check scams

messages.content: A man knocked on my door and said he was in the area and noticed my roof needs work. He wants to start today and says the price is good only right now. Should I say yes?

Please do not agree today. Being "in the area" and pushing you to decide right now are both signs of a home improvement scam.

1. Tell him you will think about it, and do not pay anything.
2. Hire only a licensed and insured contractor. Confirm the license with your state or county, and ask for proof of insurance.
3. Ask people you know and trust for recommendations.
4. Get more than one written estimate before you choose.

A real contractor can wait for you to check.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: How to avoid a home improvement scam

messages.content: Two men came by saying they had leftover paving materials from a job down the street and could do my driveway cheap. They want all the money up front, in cash, and they said I should go get the building permit from the city myself. My husband is at work so I can't ask him. It sounds like a good deal but something feels off.

Your feeling is right. Please do not pay them anything today.

1. Do not pay the full cost up front. Never make the final payment until the work is finished and you are satisfied.
2. Be careful of anyone who accepts only cash, or who asks you to get the building permits yourself.
3. Leftover materials from a previous job is another sign of this scam.
4. Wait and talk it over with your husband. A real contractor will give you a written estimate you can compare with others.

If they keep pressuring you, that is another warning sign.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: How to avoid a home improvement scam

messages.content: The contractor at my door says the repair price is only good if I sign today, and he offered to set me up with a lender he knows so I don't have to pay now. I don't have the savings. He's standing on my porch waiting. What do I do?

Do not sign anything today. Pushing for an immediate decision and offering a lender he knows are both signs of a scam.

1. Tell him you will not sign today, and close the door.
2. Do not sign anything you have not read, do not understand, or that has blank spaces.
3. If you need a loan, shop around and compare loan terms before accepting financing from a contractor.
4. Make sure you can afford the payments.
5. Do not let anyone pressure you into signing.

Never transfer your deed to anyone without first talking to an attorney or someone you trust.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: How to avoid a home improvement scam

messages.content: My elderly neighbor says a contractor keeps coming to her door pushing to fix her gutters, and wants half the money first. I want to help her without scaring her. What should I tell her?

Here is what to share with her, kindly and simply.

1. She does not have to decide right away. Pressure for an immediate decision is a sign of a scam.
2. Do not pay the full cost up front, and never make the final payment until the work is finished and she is satisfied. Some states limit how much a contractor can ask for as a down payment, so check the rules with your state or local consumer agency before she pays any deposit.
3. Use only a licensed and insured contractor. Help her confirm the license with the state or county, and ask for proof of insurance.
4. Get recommendations from people she knows and trusts, and more than one written estimate.

If something goes wrong, her state attorney general or local consumer protection office can help.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: How to avoid a home improvement scam

messages.content: How do I make sure a contractor is honest before I hire anyone to work on my house?

Take these steps before you agree to anything.

1. Use only licensed and insured contractors. Confirm the license with your state or county and ask for proof of insurance.
2. Ask people you know and trust for recommendations.
3. Check with your local Home Builders Association and consumer protection officials for complaints. Search the company name with "scam," "review," or "complaint."
4. Get several written estimates. Do not automatically pick the lowest one.
5. Read the contract carefully. It should show the contractor's name, address, phone, license number, start and finish dates, and a written statement of your right to cancel. Write in any spoken promises and fill in all blank spaces.

Do not pay everything up front.

messages.content: Someone called and said I owe money on an old account and have to pay today. I have never heard of this debt. What should I do?

Do not pay and do not share any personal or financial information on that call. First get proof that the debt is real.

1. Ask the caller to send you a written validation notice. The collector must provide it when it first contacts you or within five days after.
2. When it arrives, check the collector's name and address, the original creditor, and the amount owed.
3. If you do not owe it, send a dispute letter within 30 days. Say you do not owe the money and ask for verification of the debt.
4. Send the letter by certified mail with a return receipt, and keep a copy.

Once the collector gets your dispute, it must stop trying to collect until it sends written verification.

messages.content: A man keeps calling me at 7 in the morning and again at night, six times this week, about some credit card I don't have. He says if I don't pay he will have me arrested. I'm scared. I don't know whose debt this is and I don't want to just pay to make it stop. What are my rights?

A collector is not allowed to treat you this way, and you can dispute a debt you do not recognize.

1. Collectors cannot threaten arrest or legal action they will not take, and cannot call before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. unless you agree.
2. They also cannot harass you or call more than seven times in seven days.
3. Do not share personal or financial information until you get validation information in writing.
4. Send a letter within 30 days of getting it saying you do not owe the money, by certified mail with a return receipt.
5. If you want the calls to stop, mail the collector a letter asking it to stop contacting you. Keep a copy and send it by certified mail with a return receipt.
6. Report the calls to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov or the CFPB at cfpb.gov/complaint.

messages.content: A caller says they are suing me today unless I give my debit card number right now to settle a debt. I don't recognize it and I can't reach anyone I trust to ask. He says it's my last chance. Should I give the number?

No. Do not give your card number or any other information, and end the call.

1. Collectors cannot threaten legal action they will not take, or lie about the amount you owe.
2. Do not share personal or financial information until you have validation information in writing.
3. Ask for the written validation notice, which must arrive when they first contact you or within five days after.
4. Within 30 days of getting it, send a letter by certified mail with a return receipt. Say you do not owe the money and ask for verification of the debt.

Keep a copy of everything.

messages.content: A debt collector called my mother's friend and also called her daughter and talked about the debt. The friend says she doesn't owe it. How can I help her?

Help her avoid paying until the debt is proven, and know that a collector may not discuss her debt with her daughter.

1. A collector generally cannot discuss a debt with anyone other than her or her spouse.
2. Help her ask for a written validation notice.
3. Within 30 days of getting it, help her send a dispute letter by certified mail with a return receipt, saying she does not owe the money and asking for verification. Keep a copy.
4. Report the collector to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov, the CFPB at cfpb.gov/complaint, or her state attorney general.

She should not share personal information until the validation notice arrives.

messages.content: What can a debt collector not do, and where do I report one who breaks the rules?

Here is what a collector cannot do.

1. Harass or threaten you, or use obscene or profane language.
2. Call more than seven times in seven days, or contact you before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. unless you agree.
3. Lie about the amount owed, pretend to be an attorney or a government representative, or threaten arrest or legal action they will not take.
4. Reveal your debt publicly, or generally discuss it with anyone other than you or your spouse.

To report one, go to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov, the CFPB at cfpb.gov/complaint, or your state attorney general's office.

3. If you want the calls to end, send a letter asking the collector to stop contacting you.
4. Report the collector to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov.

Once they receive your dispute, they must stop collecting until they send written verification.

messages.content: I got a text saying I owe an unpaid toll and need to pay with a link. Is this real?

It is probably a scam. Do not tap the link or reply to the text.

1. Look up your state's tolling agency yourself and contact it with a phone number or website you know is real, not the one in the text.
2. Ask the agency whether you really owe anything.
3. Report the text with your phone's "report junk" option, or forward it to 7726 (SPAM).
4. Once you have checked it and reported it, delete the text.

Scammers want you to hurry, so it is best to stop and check.

3. If you are in doubt, call the IRS directly at 1-800-829-1040.

messages.content: A man called and said he is a U.S. Marshal and I missed jury duty, so I have to pay a fine or I will be arrested. Is that real?

Hang up. Do not give him any of the information he asks for. A federal court will never threaten you or demand immediate payment.

1. Hang up and contact your local court clerk's office or U.S. Marshals Service office.
2. Find the court's contact information at uscourts.gov/court-locator.
3. Notify the Clerk of Court's office of the U.S. District Court in your area about the call.

Jurors who miss jury duty are usually contacted by the court Clerk's Office, and any fine is imposed by a judge in open court.

messages.content: Is it okay to check my email at the coffee shop using their free Wi-Fi?

Yes, it is usually safe now. Here is how to check the website.

1. Open your email in a web browser.
2. Look at the address bar at the top.
3. Make sure you see a lock symbol or **https** in the address.

A lock symbol means the connection is encrypted, but it does not prove the website is the real one, because scammers can build fake websites that use encryption. This works on a phone browser too. Most websites use encryption these days, which is why public Wi-Fi is usually safe. Also use a strong password for your email, and turn on two-factor authentication if it is offered. Keep your phone's operating system updated, and turn on automatic updates to get the latest protections.

What should I look for so I know it is safe to type my password?

Before you type your password, look at the address bar at the top of the page. You should see a lock symbol or **https**. That means the website scrambles your information as it travels, and most websites do this now.

1. Open the website in your tablet's browser.
2. Check the address bar for the lock symbol or **https**.
3. If you see it, the connection is encrypted, but that does not prove the site is the real one, because scammers can build fake websites that use encryption.

Then sign in with a strong password. If the site offers two-factor authentication, turn it on. Keep your tablet's software updated too, and you can turn on automatic updates so it happens on its own.

3. Update your phone's operating system.

3. Look for a reseller that takes its fee after the timeshare is sold.
4. If you must pay any fee in advance, get the refund policies in writing.
5. Read the contract to check that it lists the services, the fees, and when you pay, and matches what you were told.

Do not sign if the deal is not what you expected.

If you have been scammed, report it to the FTC at ftc.gov/complaint.

messages.content: The salesman says the buyer's offer ends tomorrow, so I have to pay the $900 fee today. He says the fee is fully refundable. I really do not want to lose this buyer. What should I do?

Do not pay today because of a deadline. Take the time to check first. If you must pay in advance, get the refund policy in writing, not just by phone.

1. Contact your state Attorney General and local consumer protection agencies where the company is located, and ask about complaints.
2. Search online for complaints about the company.
3. Read the contract to make sure it lists the services, fees, and when you pay, and that it matches what he told you.
4. If the deal is not what you expected, do not sign.

It is better to deal with a reseller that takes fees after the timeshare is sold.

messages.content: My dad is 79 and wants to pay a company $2,000 to sell his timeshare. How can I help him check if it's real?

Ask him to wait before paying anything. Then you can check the company together.

1. Contact the state Attorney General and the local consumer protection agencies where the company is located. Ask whether they have complaints on file.
2. Search online for complaints about the company.
3. Look at the contract together. It should list the services, fees, and payment timing, and match what the company told him.
4. If he must pay in advance, get the refund policy in writing.

It is better to use a reseller that takes its fee after the timeshare is sold. If the deal is not what he expected, he should not sign.

messages.content: How do I pick a safe company if I ever want to sell my timeshare? And where do I report a bad one?

Check out any reseller before you agree to anything.

1. Contact your state Attorney General and local consumer protection agencies where the reseller is located. Ask whether they have complaints on file.
2. Search online for complaints.
3. Pick a reseller that takes its fees after the timeshare is sold. If you must pay in advance, get the refund policy in writing.
4. Read the contract to make sure it matches what you were told. Do not sign if the deal is not what you expected.

To report a bad company, go to ftc.gov/complaint.

messages.content: I paid a resale company $1,800 four months ago to sell my timeshare. Nothing has been sold and they stopped answering. What can I do now?

You can report this. Here is what to do.

1. Report it to the FTC at ftc.gov/complaint.

3. Search online for complaints about the company.

You did not do anything foolish. The FTC describes a company that charged an up-front fee and did not sell the property.

messages.content: A man I met on a dating site mailed me a check and asked me to wire part of it to his friend. Should I do it?

Do not forward any of the money, and stop talking to him. A fake check might clear at first, and then the bank can make you repay the full amount. Scammers use people to move stolen money, and you could get into legal trouble even if you did not know.

1. Do not send any of the money onward.
2. Stop communicating with him.
3. Report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice blog: Avoiding a money mule scam

messages.content: Someone messaged me on Facebook and said I was picked for a $5,000 grant. They want to send it to my bank account first and then have me send $1,000 back to them as a fee to their courier by gift cards. They sound very professional and I could use the help. Is this normal?

No, this is not normal. Do not forward any money, and stop communicating with this person. Scammers send money, often by check or Bitcoin, then ask you to forward part of it by gift cards or wire transfers. The money is stolen, and you could get into legal trouble for moving it. Gift cards and wire transfers are almost like sending cash, and it is almost impossible to recover the money.

1. Do not accept the grant money and send some of it onward.
2. Stop messaging the person.
3. Report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice blog: Avoiding a money mule scam

messages.content: My new online friend deposited a check in my account and it already shows as available. She says I can keep $300 and just send the rest to her cousin by wire, and not to bother the bank about it. The money is there, so it must be real, right?

Please do not send anything. A scammer's check might clear at first and still be fake. If the bank finds out later, it can make you repay the full amount, and you may face fees, an overdrawn account, or a closed account.

1. Stop the wire transfer.
2. Stop communicating with her.
3. Tell your bank right away.
4. Report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

You could also get into legal trouble if you help move stolen money, even by accident.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice blog: Avoiding a money mule scam

messages.content: My mother says her online boyfriend sends her money and she forwards some to his business partner with gift cards. I think something is wrong. What should I tell her?

Tell her to stop forwarding money and to stop communicating with him. Scammers send money, then ask people to forward it, and the money is stolen. She could get into legal trouble even if she did not know.

1. Stop any payment she can still stop.
2. Tell her bank and any gift card companies right away.
3. If he has her bank account information, close her account immediately.
4. Report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice blog: Avoiding a money mule scam

messages.content: What are the warning signs of being asked to be a money mule, so I never fall for it?

A money mule helps scammers move stolen money. Scammers find people on dating, job search, and social media sites. Watch for these:

1. Do not forward money for an online romantic interest who sends you money.
2. Do not accept a job that asks you to transfer money or packages, even if you are told it goes to a client or supplier.
3. Do not accept a grant or prize award and forward some of the money.

If you are asked, stop communicating with the person and report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice blog: Avoiding a money mule scam

messages.content: I deposited a check from an online boyfriend and sent $2,000 of it to someone he named by wire. Now my bank says the check is bad. He also has my bank account number. What do I do?

Act right away. Here is what to do.

1. Stop the payment transaction if you can.
2. Stop communicating with him.
3. Tell your bank and the wire transfer service right away.
4. He has your bank account information, so close your account immediately.
5. Report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

You may have been used to move stolen money without knowing it, so doing these steps quickly matters.

messages.content: I am moving for a new job and saw a lovely little house on a classifieds website. The owner says she is overseas on missionary work, so I cannot see the house, but she will mail me the keys once I send a deposit by Western Union. She also asked for my Social Security number for a background check. It sounds so kind. What do you think?

Please do not send the deposit or your Social Security number. A fake owner will usually claim to be out of the country when you ask to see the rental, and insisting on Western Union is another warning sign. Sending money that way is the same as sending cash, and you probably cannot get it back.

1. Until you have agreed to rent, a landlord does not need your Social Security number or other sensitive information.
2. Search the owner's name with "complaint," "review," or "scam."
3. Look up who owns the house on the city or county tax assessment website.
4. If anyone pressures you to decide quickly, walk away.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: Rental Listing Scams

messages.content: I live in another state and cannot drive over to see the apartment before I pay. The agent says I must wire the deposit by Friday or someone else gets it. How can I be sure it is real?

Do not wire the deposit by Friday. If anyone pressures you to decide quickly, walk away. Wiring money is the same as sending cash, and you probably cannot get it back. You can still check from far away.

1. Search the company's or agent's name with "complaint," "review," or "scam."
2. Check whether the property is listed on the rental company's own website.
3. Ask the agent for a business card from the company that owns or manages the property, and check the ID against the records.
4. For a private landlord, look up who owns the property on the city or county tax assessment website.
5. Contact the owner or company using contact details you already have.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: Rental Listing Scams

messages.content: My granddaughter found a cheap apartment online and the owner wants a deposit and her credit score before showing it. Is that normal?

Tell her not to pay or share anything yet. Rent that is a lot cheaper than most in the area is a sign of a scam. Also, most landlords pull your credit score themselves, so be wary of anyone asking her to get her own score for them.

1. Until she agrees to rent a place, a landlord does not need her Social Security number, credit score, or other sensitive information.
2. If she can, she should look at the property before she signs or pays.
3. Search the owner's name with "complaint," "review," or "scam."
4. Check whether the property is listed on the rental company's own website.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: Rental Listing Scams

messages.content: What are the warning signs of a fake rental ad? I want to avoid getting scammed when I search for a home.

Here are the warning signs.

1. Surprisingly low rent or amazing amenities.
2. Other ads for the same address, but with a different owner or company name.
3. An owner who claims to be out of the country when you ask to see the rental.
4. A home that is also listed for sale instead of for rent.
5. Pressure to decide quickly, or a demand to pay by wire transfer, gift cards, or cryptocurrency.

If you see any of these, walk away. To report a fake ad, tell the website where it was posted and the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: Rental Listing Scams

messages.content: I already sent $1,200 in gift cards as a deposit for an apartment and now the landlord is not answering and the ad is gone. What do I do?

I am sorry. Once you send gift cards it is probably hard to get the money back, but you should report it right away.

1. Report it to your local law enforcement agency.
2. Report it to the website where the ad was posted.
3. Report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
4. You can also report it to your state attorney general.

If you shared personal information with the scammer, the FTC has an identity theft article that can help.

messages.content: A company says they can stop my house from being foreclosed if I pay them $2,000 up front. Should I pay?

Do not pay them. Asking for money upfront, before any results, is a sign of a scam. Here is what to do.

1. Contact your servicer or lender right away, even if the foreclosure has already started.
2. Talk to a certified housing counselor for free. You can find a HUD-approved agency at apps.hud.gov/offices/hsg/sfh/hcc/hcs.cfm.
3. You can also call Making Home Affordable at 1-888-995-HOPE (4673).

It is illegal for a company to charge you a penny until it has given you a written offer for a loan modification or other relief from your lender, and you accept the offer.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: Mortgage Relief Scams

messages.content: I fell behind on my mortgage after my surgery and a man phoned saying he is a government foreclosure specialist. He wants me to sign my deed over to his company so they can hold the house safe while they fix things and he said I should stop calling my bank because it will only make things worse. He is so confident. Should I do what he says?

Please do not sign over your deed, and do not stop talking to your bank. A company cannot tell you to stop talking to your lender. Asking you to transfer the deed and claiming to be from the government are signs of a scam.

1. Contact your servicer or lender right away, even if the foreclosure has started.
2. Talk to a certified housing counselor for free. Find a HUD-approved agency at apps.hud.gov/offices/hsg/sfh/hcc/hcs.cfm.
3. Keep a file of every call, letter, email, text, and paper you receive.

messages.content: They told me not to call my lender and not to tell my counselor, or it would ruin the deal. They want a cashier's check today for $1,500. I already got a foreclosure notice and I am scared. What do I do?

Do not send the cashier's check. Scammers often tell you not to contact your lender or housing counselor, and no company can tell you to stop talking to your lender. Do not pay anything until a company delivers the results you want.

1. Contact your servicer or lender right away. You can do this even if the foreclosure process has already started.
2. Talk to a certified housing counselor for free. Find a HUD-approved agency at apps.hud.gov/offices/hsg/sfh/hcc/hcs.cfm.
3. You can also call 1-888-995-HOPE (4673).

messages.content: How do I spot a mortgage relief scam, and where do I report one?

Watch for these signs.

1. They demand payment upfront, before any services.
2. They want payment only by cashier's check, wire transfer, or a mobile payment app.
3. They try to get you to transfer your deed to them.
4. They tell you not to contact your lender, lawyer, or housing counselor.
5. They claim to be housing counselors, lawyers, or government representatives.

To report one, go to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov, or contact your state attorney general.
